- typed param: `export function render(validate: () => void) { validate(); }`
- untyped param: `export function render2(useAuto) { useAuto(); }`

**P2 — `VARIABLE_DECLARATOR_RE` mis-captures typed declarators (over- and under-capture).**

Running a declarator regex over the `export const` RHS misfires both ways. **Over-capture** (the worse half — invents export names that then drive false edges):

**2. The query never calls `normalizeFtsText`.** The write path composes `normalizeFtsText(applyCjkSegmentationIfEnabled(text))` (collapses `\r\n\t` to a space), but this query path only calls `applyCjkSegmentationIfEnabled(query)` — confirmed by direct grep, `normalizeFtsText` never appears in this file. Two C++-specific assumptions don't hold for Java: (1) if the nearest class in the MRO declares any overload of the name but none match arity, the walk stops entirely with no edge — Java doesn't hide inherited overloads this way; (2) method lookup unconditionally precedes field lookup, but Java fields/methods can share a name (e.g. records synthesize accessor `x()` alongside field `x`) — a `this.x` field read could resolve to the method instead.

One review lane instrumented the actual pipeline for both scenarios: on today's code, HEAD and BASE produce the *same* (independently wrong, pre-existing) output — not because Case 0.5 is safe, but because two *unrelated* bugs (a duplicate tree-sitter reference-site match, and an old Case-4 arity-blind shortcut) happen to currently mask it. The cited precedent (`getNpmMajorVersion`, `cli/resolve-invocation.ts`) is only safe because it passes `['--version']` — no paths, no ranges.

**P2 — COBOL/JCL exact snippets are off-by-one / wrong-line.**

This exact-path slice treats `startLine`/`endLine` as **0-based** array indices. That holds for tree-sitter symbols (`parse-worker.ts:2312` is 0-based), but **COBOL and JCL emit 1-based line numbers**, and every label they produce is in `EXACT_SYMBOL_CONTENT_LABELS`. So their stored FTS `content` is shifted by one: multi-line symbols drop their own declaration line and bleed one trailing line; **single-line** symbols (JCL Job/Step/DD, COBOL data items / EXEC blocks) store the **wrong line entirely**, or an **empty string** when the symbol is on the file's last physical line.

**Evidence:** 1-based source at `cobol-preprocessor.ts:1142` and `jcl-parser.ts:131` (`const lineNum = i + 1;`) flows to `cobol-processor.ts:480` (Function `para.line`), `:362` (Module hardcoded `startLine: 1`), `:445` (Namespace `sec.line`), `:514` (Property `item.line`), `:617` (CodeElement `call.line`), and `jcl-processor.ts:101/140/212/247` (CodeElement/Module). A first-line JCL JOB stores `lines[1]` instead of `lines[0]`. The old `Math.max(0, startLine-2)` window accidentally compensated for the +1 offset (it always reached index ≥0), so this is a **regression** exposed by removing the ±2 buffer for these labels.

**Fix:** normalize the COBOL/JCL emitters to 0-based (`-1`; full-file span `endLine: lines.length-1`) so they match every other emitter — the root-cause fix — **or** keep those labels on the ±2 window / exclude them from the exact path until their ranges are normalized. Caveat: `findOwningProgramName` / `findContainingSection` compare a `line` value against `startLine` from the **same** 1-based source, so normalize **both sides together** and check the route-containment / MCP-display consumers before flipping.

_Cross-engine: both engines, 5 lanes (claude risk-architect + ce-correctness; codex swarm + ce + adversarial). Coordinator-verified. `[code-read]` — no COBOL/JCL index was executed; confirm against a real mainframe index if precision matters._

**HIGH — incremental writeback persists a stale bean attribution; incremental and full rebuild diverge.**

`frameworkAnnotations` is (as far as I can find) the first persisted node *property* whose value depends on **other files'** content: the wildcard leg consults package siblings injected by `populateJavaPackageSiblings`. But the incremental write set is edge-based — changed files ∪ importer-BFS over `IMPORTS` edges (`subgraph-extract.ts` walks edges only; no property diffing) — and Java same-package implicit visibility produces no `IMPORTS` edge.

**Reproduced with this PR's built CLI:**
1. Full analyze of `package com.other; import org.springframework.stereotype.*; @Service public class WildcardService {}` → row = `["org.springframework.stereotype.Service"]` (correct — the wildcard fixture asserts exactly this).
2. Add `com/other/Service.java`: `package com.other; public @interface Service {}` (per JLS 6.4.1 the package member now shadows the on-demand import). Incremental analyze logs `changed=0, added=1 … 1 unchanged file rows preserved` → row **still** `["org.springframework.stereotype.Service"]`.
3. `analyze --force` on the identical tree → `[]` (correct).

This pass recomputes the right answer in memory each run — but the recomputed value never reaches the DB for unchanged files, so `context`/`impact` report a Spring bean indefinitely until something else touches that file. The symmetric direction (deleting the shadow type) leaves a stale under-report. The `INCREMENTAL_SCHEMA_VERSION` 6→7 bump only covers the upgrade top-up, not ongoing runs.

**Remediation options:** (a) when the changed/added/deleted set (re)declares a top-level Java type whose simple name is one of the six stereotype simple names, seed that package's other `.java` files into the write set (cheap — six names); or (b) diff computed `frameworkAnnotations` against the pre-run Class rows and pull mismatches into the effective write set.

**MEDIUM — the wildcard leg fails open on three legal-Java shadowing channels, attributing the wrong bean (the direction this PR itself treats as severe).**

The three gates (lexical scope chain, explicit imports, visible bindings) miss:

1. **Inherited member annotation types** (JLS 6.3 + 6.4.1): `class Base { @interface Service {} } class Holder extends Base { @Service static class Inner {} }` with a lone `import org.springframework.stereotype.*;` — javac binds `Base.Service`, but no gate consults the resolved EXTENDS/MRO chain, so `Inner` gets attributed Spring's `Service`.
2. **Single-static-import of an external nested annotation type**: `import static app.Annotations.Service;` shadows on-demand imports, but static imports are interpreted as `kind:'named'` **without** `targetIncludesImportedName` (see the `static` case in `interpret.ts`), so `explicitImportTargets` skips them; if `app.Annotations` is an external JAR, `hasVisibleTypeBinding` sees nothing either → Spring attributed.
3. **Packages over the sibling cap**: `populateJavaPackageSiblings` disables same-package visibility beyond `MAX_PACKAGE_FILES = 500` (`package-siblings.ts:80-89`), and this suppression path depends entirely on that channel — in a >500-file package the gate silently fails *open*, not closed.

All three need an annotation type named exactly like a stereotype plus a lone Spring wildcard — rare, but each is compiling Java recorded wrongly. Fixtures cover lexical/top-level/member/package-sibling/explicit/multi-wildcard shadows only.

**Remediation:** in this leg, fail closed when (i) *any* named/alias `ParsedImport` binds the simple name regardless of `targetIncludesImportedName`, (ii) the class has a resolved superclass whose owned members include the simple name (the MRO machinery already exists), and (iii) the file's package was sibling-capped (have `populateJavaPackageSiblings` report capped packages).

**[MEDIUM] Naive comma-split breaks on multi-arg generic interfaces**

`emitExtensionImplementsHeritage` splits the `implements` clause text on every comma, so a multi-type-argument generic interface gets split mid-generic and emits a spurious extra IMPLEMENTS edge.

Empirically reproduced against this PR's code:
```dart
class Comparator<A, B> {}

extension type Pair(String a) implements Comparator<String, int> {
  String describe() => a;
}
```
produces **two** heritage markers instead of one:
- `implements:Comparator:Pair` (correct)
- `implements:int:Pair` (bogus — `Pair` does not implement `int`)

The pre-existing structural heritage path for regular classes (`emitHeritageMarkers`, ~line 550 in this same file) doesn't have this problem because it walks the AST's `type_identifier` named children instead of parsing raw text — tree-sitter already segments `Comparator` from its `<String, int>` type_arguments as separate children. `extension_declaration` has no `interfaces` field in the vendored grammar (checked `vendor/tree-sitter-dart/src/node-types.json`), which is presumably why this fell back to text parsing — but the fallback needs to be bracket-depth-aware when splitting on commas (skip commas nested inside `<...>`).

Not covered by the new tests — the fixture only exercises single-arg generics (`SequenceLike<T>`). Suggest adding a regression case with a 2-arg generic interface alongside the fix.

**[MEDIUM — regression] Wildcard-import files lose all `@Autowired` collection-injection edges.**

`SPRING_DI_CAPTURED_FIELD_PROPERTY` is stamped here for **every** syntactically-captured field (`hasRelevantAnnotation` = simple-name match on `Autowired`/`Inject`), *before* and *independent of* FQN resolution. It suppresses the legacy collection matcher at `di-extractors/spring.ts:284`. But an edge is only emitted if semantic resolution succeeds — and `createSpringAnnotationNameResolver` returns `undefined` when a file has 2+ wildcard imports (`frameworks/spring/bean-candidates.ts:166`, `wildcardPackages.size !== 1`). When they diverge, the field is suppressed *and* produces nothing.

Reproduced end-to-end on a built checkout of the head — identical `@Autowired private List<IFoo> foos;`:
```
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;  → Consumer->FooA, Consumer->FooB
import java.util.*;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.*;           → (no edges)
```
A second probe confirmed it's a regression: on the wildcard node the retained `springDiFieldMatcher(node)` still matches (pre-PR that emitted both edges), yet the captured flag is set and 0 INJECTS edges exist. Broader collateral: when a `@Service` stereotype *itself* arrives via wildcard, `frameworkAnnotations` never gets set, so the whole class disappears from DI (no constructor/field/setter injection either). No test uses wildcard imports.

**Fix:** gate the marker on a *successfully-emitted* match rather than on syntactic capture — accumulate resolved field names inside the site loop and stamp `SPRING_DI_CAPTURED_FIELD_PROPERTY` only for those after `matches` is built, so the legacy fallback still fires when the new path yields nothing for a field.

**[LOW] `defaultBeanName` diverges from Spring's `Introspector.decapitalize` for digit-second-char names.**

`className[1] !== className[1].toUpperCase()` treats a digit as uppercase (`'1'.toUpperCase() === '1'`), so the first char isn't lowercased. Probe-confirmed divergences: `S3Client`→`S3Client`, `H2Repository`→`H2Repository`, `X509Cert`→`X509Cert` — where Spring yields `s3Client`/`h2Repository`/`x509Cert`. Since this default name feeds `@Qualifier` matching (`pipeline-phases/di.ts:203`), `@Qualifier("s3Client")` against an unnamed `S3Client` provider silently mismatches and the edge drops. Common in AWS/H2/versioned-API code.

**Fix:** use Java's actual rule — leave unchanged only when both `name[0]` and `name[1]` are uppercase *letters*, e.g. `className[1] === className[1].toLowerCase()` as the not-uppercase test (a digit equals its own lowercase → decapitalize). Guard `length === 0` while here (`defaultBeanName('')` currently throws, though unreachable today).

**[LOW — DoD] `SCHEMA_BUMP` bumped 20→21 without a `v21:` changelog entry.**

The comment block just above documents every prior bump (v16–v20) and this file's own contract says any `ParsedFile` serialization change "MUST bump `SCHEMA_BUMP`" — the *why* is the convention. The bump itself is correct and load-bearing (it's what invalidates pre-PR ParsedFiles so unchanged files re-parse and gain `springDiFacts` on the first run); only the note is missing.

**Fix:** add e.g. `// v21: Java Spring DI facts (constructor/field/method injection sites + bean/@Primary provider metadata) added to the capture side-channel.`

**[LOW] Empty-parenthesis stereotype (`@Service()`, `@Component()`) yields a nameless provider.**

For `@Service()`, `annotation.text.includes('(')` is true, `staticStringArgument('@Service()')` returns `undefined` (no string literal), so `hasDynamicBeanName = true` and the default-name branch is skipped → `provider.names = []`. Probe-confirmed: `@Service` → `["fooService"]` but `@Service()` → `[]`. In Spring `@Service()` ≡ `@Service` (default name applies), so `@Qualifier("fooService")` against such a bean mismatches and drops the edge.

**Fix:** treat an empty/whitespace-only argument list as "no explicit name" (fall through to `defaultBeanName`); set `hasDynamicBeanName` only for a genuinely non-empty non-literal value.

**[LOW — behavioral change] Class-and-Interface same-name fail-closed alters pre-existing collection behavior.**

The old phase indexed only interfaces, so `@Autowired List<FooService>` resolved to a unique `interface FooService` and fanned out regardless of any same-named class. This gate now skips (`ambiguousSkipped++`) when a name resolves to **both** a Class and an Interface — so in a repo with `interface FooService` plus an unrelated `class FooService` in another package, that injection emitted edges before and emits nothing now.

The fail-closed choice is defensible (a graph-only phase can't tell which type the site meant) and the concrete-class resolution this index enables is a real improvement — it only bites on true simple-name collisions. But it's a behavior change not called out in the PR description and covered only by the new positive unit test, not this regression path. Please document it (and ideally add a regression fixture).

The file backend is immune (`O_EXCL` → inode). Fix: `realpathSync` the deepest existing ancestor before hashing (fall back to `path.resolve` only when nothing on the path exists yet). Reproduced via `repro-symlink.mjs`: both aliases acquired the socket lock. (Cross-netns containers sharing a bind-mount are a *separate*, already-documented limitation this fix does not address.)

This directly contradicts the module header's promise to re-check freshness *after* acquiring the lock. Self-heals on the next analyze, but serves a stale index silently until then. On the default Linux/Windows backend that's the *only* path a timeout takes. Fix here at the socket call site (not the shared `unknownHolder()` helper — the file backend also uses it at :450/:463): emit `null`/omit the pid for the socket backend and have the CLI print "another process (pid unknown)".

module.exports = { run() { this.helper(); }, helper() {} };   // object-literal: edge lost
const X = class { m() { this.n(); } n() {} };                 // class expression: edge lost

**P1 — module identity drops the crate, so this can silently switch the fix off in a cargo workspace.** `[reproduced]`

`moduleOfFile` returns only the segments below a crate root, and `sameModule` (line 137) compares only those segments. Re-run directly:

```
crateRoots: ["crates/a/src", "crates/b/src"]
crates/a/src/tools.rs -> ["tools"]
crates/b/src/tools.rs -> ["tools"]   # identical
```

**Trigger:** a workspace where two members each have `src/tools.rs`. If only one defines the member you get a wrong **cross-crate** edge; if both do, `findMemberInModule` sees `count === 2`, refuses, and the site falls back to the lexical chain — **restoring the exact #2730 self-loop**.

Same-named modules across members (`util`, `error`, `config`, `types`) are near-universal, and **#2730's own repro repo is multi-crate** (`crates/noob`, `crates/noob-provider`), while `rust-2730-crate-layout` has a single member and so cannot catch either manifestation.

**Fix:** make module identity `{ crateRoot, segments }` and thread it through member and re-export lookup.

**P1 — the `use`-binding channel accepts an imported TYPE as a module.** `[reproduced]`

Nothing checks that `head` names a module. `tryRustModulePath` *deliberately* strips a trailing symbol segment (`import-resolvers/rust.ts:77` — "last segment might be a symbol… Strip it and try again"), so:

```rust
use crate::client::ClientBuilder;   // edge -> targetFile = src/client/mod.rs
ClientBuilder::new()                // candidate module becomes ["client"]
```

Rust impl methods carry a **bare** `qualifiedName` (`function_item` captures only `@declaration.name`), so the tail is then looked up as an ordinary module member.

Many such calls land correctly by accident — when the impl method is the only callable of that name in the module. The failure is conditional but structural: a **false edge** when a module-level callable of the same name also exists (`new`, `default`, `from`, `build`, `load`, `parse` in a facade `mod.rs` — exactly the shape `pub use` motivates), or a misfire into the tie-refuse path when several do.

**Fix:** require the `use`-channel head to resolve to an actual module before accepting it.

_Reproduced independently by two Claude lanes with separate drivers._

**P1 — membership is inferred from file path alone, so one nested helper disables qualified resolution for the whole module.** `[reproduced]`

This loop counts every def whose `moduleOfDef` matches, with no check that the def is owned by a **module-level** scope. A `fn` nested inside another `fn`, or an `impl`/trait method (both carry bare `qualifiedName`s), counts as a second module member.

**Trigger:** the target module contains a function-local `fn dispatch` — or an `impl X { fn dispatch }` — alongside the real `pub fn dispatch`. `count === 2` → refuse → the site is handed back to the tier that emits the wrong self-loop, **reinstating #2730**, with no resolution outcome recorded.

The refuse-on-tie *logic* is correct (I checked: the multi-match value is genuinely discarded and the index dedups `(name, DefId)`); the problem is what is being counted.

**Fix:** restrict candidates to defs owned by a module-level scope.

_Found by **both engines** — Claude adversarial reproduced it on the #2730 shape verbatim; Codex adversarial and Codex CE reached it independently by source read._

**P1 — full workspace scan per candidate, on a path taken by every `Path::name()` call.** `[reproduced]`

This walks all of `workspaceIndex.moduleScopeByFile` with no module→file index, once per candidate. Combined with the capture at `query.ts:172` matching **any** `scoped_identifier` callee, the hook runs for `Vec::new()`, `String::from()`, `HashMap::new()` — calls that can never resolve into the workspace but pay `O(defs-named-X + files)` each before returning `undefined`.

Two independent benchmarks agree per-site cost is linear in file count:
- 0.117 → 0.228 → 0.428 ms/site at 301 / 601 / 1201 files
- 0.26 → 9.46 ms/call at N=500 → 16,000

Total pass cost is O(qualified-call-sites x file-count). Given the #2649 / #1871 history this is worth fixing before merge.

**Fix:** build a `Map<modulePathKey, Scope>` once per pass (or add `moduleScopeByModulePath` to `WorkspaceResolutionIndex`), and skip the hook when the qualifier head cannot name a workspace module.

_Note: under `GITNEXUS_DISK_SCOPE_INDEX=1` (default-off) this walk runs after the scope-tree seal, turning the CPU scan into per-file `readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` — the exact pattern `exportedCallableByName` was added to avoid._

**P2 — candidate 1 is an unchecked guess yielded before the `use` channel.**

`[...callerModule, ...qualifier]` never verifies the caller actually declares that submodule, so file layout beats a real `use` binding.

**Trigger:** `src/a/mod.rs` has `use crate::b;` while an undeclared (or `cfg`-gated) `src/a/b.rs` exists — candidate 1 matches `['a','b']` first and wins. rustc would resolve to `crate::b`.

**Fix:** only yield candidate 1 when `qualifier[0]` is genuinely a declared submodule of the caller (an import edge with that `localName`, or an inline `Namespace` scope).

**P2 — the C++-era "already namespaced" guard mis-fires for Rust.** `[reproduced]`

`tagNamespacePrefixes` skips a def when its `qualifiedName` already equals or starts with the prefix (`walkers.ts:1054`, `:1078`). That guard was written for C++, where `qualifiedName` carries the namespace. In Rust it means `fn a` inside `mod a` — or `mod inner { fn inner }` — keeps `namespacePrefix` **unset**, so `moduleOfDef` reports it as a member of the *parent* module.

**Trigger:** `pub mod a { pub fn a() {} }` then `crate::a::a()` — refuses. Worse, that def is then indistinguishable from a crate-root `fn a` for the module matcher.

**[P1] Two lexical desyncs wedge the scanner inside multiline-string state, silently making the fix inert for the rest of the file.**

Measured on a fixed template (class + multiline string + a real indented `#if`/`#endif` in the same body), asking only whether the *real* directives got blanked:

```
control : plain string, plain close            directivesBlanked=true
(a)     : escaped \""" inside the string        directivesBlanked=false
(b)     : close """ immediately followed by #   directivesBlanked=false
control2: close """ then SPACE then #           directivesBlanked=true
```

**(a)** The multiline-string branch at lines 63-72 has no escape handling, unlike `skipRegularString` at line 39. Swift's documented `\"""` is read as the closing delimiter; the scanner then re-enters string state at the *real* `"""` and never leaves. It also blanks directive-looking lines *inside* the string literal, rewriting the program's string data — the exact invariant the new unit test at `:64-101` asserts must hold.

**(b)** This line — `if (poundCount === 0) return line[index + 3] === '#' ? 0 : 3;` — refuses to close a **plain** `"""` string whenever a `#` immediately follows. `control2` (a space before the `#`) blanks correctly, which isolates the adjacency as the cause. The `poundCount > 0` guard at line 25 is correct; generalizing it down to N=0 is not — a bare `"""` always closes a plain multiline string. The same over-strict guard also refuses `"""##` as a terminator for a `#"""` string.

Both fail silently: length is preserved, nothing errors, the fix just does nothing for that file and the original class-body-drop bug returns.

**Fix:** in the `multilineStringPounds !== null` branch, skip backslash escapes when the count is 0 (mirroring `skipRegularString`); and drop the `#`-adjacency guards here — `poundCount === 0` ⇒ `return 3`, and for `poundCount > 0` accept a terminator with at least `poundCount` pounds. **[P2] The predicate keys on indentation, but the grammar's acceptance keys on nesting — so the fix misses the common case and over-fires on the documented one.**

`^[ \t]+` requires leading whitespace, and the doc comment at lines 119-120 justifies it with *"Top-level directives are left intact because they are valid source-file members in the grammar."* Column 0 and top level are not the same thing, in either direction.

**Miss:** a `#if` at column 0 *inside* a class body is left untouched and the class is still discarded. Measured over 7 body shapes (enum member, nested struct, property, func, typealias, nested class, empty body), 6 lose the enclosing declaration:

```
COL0    enum member   blanked=false  hasError=true   classCaptured=false
INDENT  enum member   blanked=true   hasError=false  classCaptured=true
```

An A/B pipeline run confirms base and PR are byte-identical for that fixture — the fix is a no-op there. This is common formatting (SwiftFormat `--ifdef outdent`, Xcode re-indent), so it is a large share of the real-world population.

**Over-fire:** an *indented* directive at file scope **is** blanked, e.g. a valid `  #if DEBUG` at top level — contrary to the sentence above and to the contract the new integration test claims to pin.

Same-root variants that widen the miss: NBSP or ideographic-space indentation, a UTF-8 BOM before a first-line directive, and CR-only line endings (line 144 splits on `\n` only, so such a file is treated as one line and nothing matches).

**Fix:** decide on nesting depth, not indentation. `scanSwiftLine` already walks every character and already skips strings and comments, so it can maintain a `braceDepth` for free; blank any `#if|#elseif|#else|#endif` line when `braceDepth > 0` at line start, regardless of leading whitespace. That preserves today's verified top-level behavior and subsumes the whitespace variants. Failing that, at minimum correct the doc comment to say "unindented" rather than "top-level", and add the column-0-inside-a-body matrix as a regression table.

**[P1] Blanking is unconditional, so an `#if`/`#else` that branches a declaration *header* leaves unbalanced braces and re-parents the rest of the file.**

Swift legitimately splits one declaration header across branches — availability and cross-platform code does this routinely:

```swift
class NetworkClient {
  #if swift(>=5.5)
  func fetch() async {
  #else
  func fetch() {
  #endif
    perform()
  }
}

struct SessionStore {}
enum Unrelated { case a }
```

Both branch bodies open a brace; only one closes. Blanking both markers leaves two `{` and one `}`, so `NetworkClient` never closes. Measured against the real vendored grammar — top-level node lists:

```
RAW          top-level: class_declaration, directive, function_declaration,
                        class_declaration, class_declaration
PREPROCESSED top-level: class_declaration
```

Five top-level declarations collapse to one; `SessionStore` and `Unrelated` stop being top level and get reparented under `NetworkClient`. A separate A/B pipeline run measured the graph consequence directly: `qn="SessionStore"` → `qn="NetworkClient.SessionStore"` (same for `TokenCache`, `Config`, `Environment`), and `NetworkClient`'s span grew from one line to the whole file. `qualifiedName` is what resolution, `context` and `rename` key on.

Be precise about the severity: both sides have `hasError=true` here, because the raw form is the very bug this PR targets. So this is not "valid → invalid" — it is **partially-recovered → structurally wrong**, with unrelated types silently reparented. Today's failure is local to the affected declaration; after this change it is file-global, and nothing detects it.

**Fix:** don't blank a directive group whose branches have unequal net `{`/`}` counts — degrade to today's behavior for that group rather than emitting an unbalanced file. A `braceDepth` counter in `scanSwiftLine` (see the nesting-vs-indentation comment on line 1) gives you the raw material for both checks at once. Add this shape as a regression, asserting `qualifiedName` and spans, not just the set of definition names — the existing check that reported "definition set identical" missed this precisely because it compared names only.

**P2 `[reproduced]` — O(depth²) build, unbounded recursion, and a pure receiver *miss* now pays for both.**

This calls `collectNamespaceMembers` for **every** `Namespace` scope, not just roots. In a chain `outer { inline v1 { inline v2 { … } } }` each of `outer`, `v1`, `v2` … is itself a legal receiver (`v2::foo()` is valid C++), so each is visited by this loop and re-descends its remaining descendants via :222-224 — D + (D−1) + … + 1.

Measured build time over a depth sweep: 0.284 ms @ 50, 2.404 ms @ 200, 7.789 ms @ 400, 27.463 ms @ 800, 114.2 ms @ 1600 — exponent **1.94** (400→1600) and **1.86** (200→1600), the O(D²) signature.

Harder edge, separately reproduced: resolving a receiver that **does not exist** costs 5.1 ms at depth 100, 428.3 ms at depth 5000, and throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` at depth 10000. That throw is uncontained — `run.ts`'s only `try/catch` wraps the CFG/PDG emit block, and `phase.ts:324`'s `try` has a `finally` with no `catch` — so it aborts the whole analyze (same failure class as #2769).

**This part is a genuine delta of the PR:** the deleted walker recursed only for namespaces whose simple name matched the query (`if (nsName !== receiverName) continue;`), so a miss cost zero recursion. The new build reaches every namespace regardless of what is queried.

**Suggested fix:** thread a `depth` counter (or a visited-`ScopeId` set) into `collectNamespaceMembers` and bail with a `logger.warn` past a generous ceiling — that closes both the stack overflow and the pathological build in a few lines. If the O(D²) itself is worth removing, process inline scopes bottom-up and memoize each scope's transitive member map.

'complete' : …`), both outside this diff. **Trigger, and it is a deterministic ordering rather than a race:** `runEmbeddingPipeline` emits `phase:'ready'`/`percent:100` unconditionally before returning (`embedding-pipeline.ts:867-872`), including when `failedNodeIds.size > 0`. So the sequence is always (1) `ready` → mapped to `complete`, (2) `mountSSEProgress` writes `event: complete` with `error: undefined`, `res.end()`, `unsubscribe()`, (3) only then does this block compute `partialRunError` and call `updateJob({status:'failed'})` — into a stream with no listener. `gitnexus-web` has already fired `onComplete` and set the UI to `ready`. **This is a regression in the PR's own headline claim:** pre-PR a failing sub-batch threw, the pipeline emitted `phase:'error'` → mapped to `'failed'`, and the client received it. `GET /api/embed/:jobId` pollers are unaffected, so the two consumers now disagree. **Fix:** stop mapping the pipeline's `ready` to a terminal SSE phase (map it to e.g. `finalizing` and let this explicit `updateJob` be the only terminal event — `updateJob` already synthesizes `{phase:'complete',percent:100}` for a status change), or make `mountSSEProgress` close on the terminal job **status** rather than a progress phase string. Found by two Claude lanes; all three Codex legs missed it and one explicitly refuted it — the coordinator verified the full chain. [code-read]

**P1 — the unknown-count fallback reads a run-START snapshot, so it can overwrite a newer measured count with a stale zero and arm an embedding wipe.** `existingMeta` is assigned exactly once, at line 934, before any embedding work; this fallback therefore republishes the pre-run figure and can clobber the fresher count the terminal `onCheckpoint` already wrote to disk during this same run. **Trigger:** (1) existing meta says `stats.embeddings: 0`, or omits it; (2) a clean `analyze --embeddings` (or `/api/embed`) successfully inserts embeddings; (3) the final count query is unavailable — a transient failure after the terminal checkpoint count already succeeded; (4) finalization carries the old zero forward *and* clears the checkpoint, reporting success; (5) a later `analyze --force` reads `0` → `embedding-mode.ts:69` `hasExisting` false → `forceRegenerateEmbeddings` false → `shouldLoadCache` false → the rebuild destroys the live embeddings. The comment directly above says a wrong-LOW value is the dangerous direction — this path produces one. **Fix:** fall back to the latest *checkpoint* metadata rather than the run-start snapshot, and when embeddings were attempted but no finite count can be verified, retain an identity-matching recovery checkpoint (even with an empty pending set) instead of clearing it. Add a regression seeded with prior count `0` + an unanswerable final query that asserts the next `--force` still loads the cache. Found by both Codex legs (98% / 75%) and by no Claude lane; coordinator-confirmed. [code-read]

**P1 — a successful, exit-0 partial run now plants a checkpoint that hard-aborts later routine runs, and `--force` cannot clear it.** This block writes `pendingEmbeddingCheckpoint` (stamped with this run's `provider`, which is `http:<sha256(safeUrl(GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_URL))>` in HTTP mode per `embedding-identity.ts:19-23`) into the final success-shaped meta at 2847. **Trigger:** `GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_URL=… gitnexus analyze --embeddings` drops three nodes to a transient endpoint fault, warns, and **exits 0** with the checkpoint persisted. **P2 — a short or empty `data` array passes this shape check, so the very body class the PR set out to retry still gets one attempt and still resets the breaker.** `payload.data.every(isEmbeddingItem)` is vacuously true for `[]` and true for any array shorter than the request. **P2 — this catch swallows *every* rejection from `.json()`, not just parse errors, so a body-phase timeout is retried 3×, charged to the shared circuit breaker, and misreported as "unparseable".** `RetryableEmbeddingBodyError` is a plain `Error`, so it defeats `classifyOutcome`'s DOMException check (`resilient-fetch.ts:96-101`) and lands in `retryable-network` — which retries and calls `breaker.recordFailure()` (`:250-253`) — instead of `terminal-network`, whose documented contract is "returned without retry AND without incrementing the breaker" via `recordNeutral()` (`:225-232`). **Reproduced** with a throwaway probe at `GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3`: a `TimeoutError` DOMException raised inside `.json()` → **3 fetch calls**, message *"Embedding endpoint returned an unparseable response"*; the identical error raised from `fetch()` itself → **1 call**, message *"Embedding request timed out after 180000ms"*. Same error object, same policy question, opposite behaviour purely because of when it is raised. **Trigger:** a buffering proxy that flushes `200 OK` immediately then stalls the body — 3× the timeout and 3× the endpoint's GPU work per sub-batch, and because `CircuitBreaker.failureThreshold` defaults to 3, three such sub-batches open the process-global `embeddings-http` breaker (shared with interactive `httpEmbedQuery` in the server), which the pre-PR `recordNeutral()` path explicitly avoided. The operator is then shown "unparseable response" and will never reach for `GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS` — the misdiagnosis class #2386 added the typed boundary to close. **Fix:** `if (err instanceof DOMException && (err.name === 'TimeoutError' || err.name === 'AbortError')) throw err;` before wrapping, and move the `RetryableEmbeddingBodyError` branch in the outer catch after the `TimeoutError` branch. Note the interaction with `isCancellationError`: re-raising a bare `AbortError` must be checked against the caller's own signal, not the error name alone, or a transport abort becomes a false cancel. [reproduced]

**P2 — the ratio guard cannot fire below its own 20-sub-batch floor, and a resume run is always below it.** `MIN_SUB_BATCHES_BEFORE_FAILURE_RATIO_GUARD = 20` needs 20 sub-batches ≈ 160 chunks ≈ ~80 embeddable nodes at the default `subBatchSize: 8` — the file's own comment at 350-351 states the 160-chunk figure ("At the default `subBatchSize` of 8 the floor is ~160 chunks of evidence before the rate can abort anything"), which is what makes the dead zone verifiable rather than speculative. **Trigger:** a 50-node repo whose endpoint rejects every other sub-batch fails 5 of 10 — a 50% loss rate — but `10 < 20` blocks the ratio guard, and every intervening success resets `consecutiveSubBatchFailures`, so the ceiling of 5 never trips either. ~25 nodes are silently dropped and `analyze` exits 0. The floor is a deliberate and well-argued choice for a *first* run over a small repo (one failure out of one sub-batch is 100% and means nothing), so this is not an objection to the shape — it is that **every resume run has exactly this shape by construction**: its node set is only the pending ids, so it produces few sub-batches no matter how large the repo is, and the guard that exists to stop a degraded endpoint from eating the corpus is structurally off in the one run whose entire purpose is retrying against that endpoint. Compounds with the non-convergence in the `run-analyze.ts:2612` finding. Separately, and by design rather than by defect: any steady loss rate below 25% never aborts, so a single run may drop up to a quarter of the corpus and still exit 0 behind one warning line — worth stating in the docs the docs-gap section asks for. **Fix:** scale the floor to the run rather than fixing it (e.g. `Math.max(5, Math.ceil(totalNodes / 16))` computed before the loop), or bound the absolute number of nodes one run may drop, so a resume run is judged on its own terms. Two Claude lanes. [code-read]

**Blocking.** This is the only surface a one-click user reads, and "with no API keys required" reads as a convenience feature when it actually describes the absence of authentication.

`render.yaml:6-8` says the right thing and says it plainly — unauthenticated, `onrender.com` names show up in certificate transparency logs, rate limits are not access control. Render renders the blueprint's resources, not its comments, so none of that reaches the person clicking the badge.

I stood up `gitnexus serve --host 0.0.0.0` locally with both new variables set exactly as this blueprint sets them. Every write route accepted an `Origin`-less request: `POST /api/analyze {"path":"/etc"}` returned `202` with a jobId, and `DELETE /api/repo`, `DELETE /api/analyze/:jobId`, `DELETE /api/embed/:jobId`, `POST /api/analyze/upload` and `POST /api/mcp` `initialize` all passed the guard. The read routes have no guard either, so every visitor can read every indexed repo's source.

Either ship the blueprint authenticated by default — `resolveAuthToken` and `timingSafeEqual` already exist in `http-transport.ts`, and Render has `generateValue: true`, so a token generated for the server and handed to `gitnexus-web` via `fromService` is a small change — or put an unmissable callout right here carrying the substance of `render.yaml:6-8`, and drop the Azure PAT keys from a public blueprint either way.

**Blocking.** This sample value is the API server's own hostname, but the variable is compared against the browser's `Origin` request header — the origin of the *page* making the call.

The web UI calls the API cross-origin via `backendUrl` (`gitnexus-web/src/config/ui-constants.ts:6`, `hooks/useBackend.ts:29`), so the correct value is the **web UI's** URL. That is exactly what `render.yaml:43-47` wires, from `gitnexus-web`'s `RENDER_EXTERNAL_URL` — the blueprint is right and the docs are backwards. `README.md:521` and the runtime warning at `api.ts:767` ("set `GITNEXUS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` to its public origin", where "its" is the server) read the same way.

Since `Dockerfile.cli` is API-only, the two origins are always different on a split deploy, so the documented reading is always wrong there. I confirmed the consequence locally: set to the server's own URL, requests from the UI origin get no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on reads and `403 origin_not_allowed` on writes — a blank UI — while the one origin that works is the one no browser is on.

Suggest rewording all three to describe the caller ("the origin of the web UI that will call this server — the page origin browsers load, not this server's own URL; in a single-service deploy where `serve` also serves the UI they are the same"), changing this sample to a UI hostname, and pointing at `render.yaml`'s `fromService` block as the worked example. Worth also saying out loud that the bare-host form admits `http://` as well as `https://` (`middleware.ts:78-80`) — harmless for the shipped blueprint since `RENDER_EXTERNAL_URL` carries the scheme, but this example is what a TLS deploy will copy.

**Blocking.** This gates the warning on the matcher being *constructible*, not on it being able to match anything — so setting `GITNEXUS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` **wrong** is diagnosed strictly worse than leaving it unset.

`normalizeBoundHost` goes through `new URL('http://' + host)`, and WHATWG hostname parsing for special schemes accepts a lot of things that are not hostnames. I ran these against the real `createPublicOriginMatcher` — all truthy, all unmatchable:

```
"https://a.onrender.com,https://b.onrender.com"  truthy  expects hostname "a.onrender.com,https"
"https://*.onrender.com"                         truthy  expects hostname "*.onrender.com"
"2001:db8::1:8443"                               truthy  expects hostname "[2001:db8::1:8443]"
"1"                                              truthy  expects hostname "0.0.0.1"
"*"                                              truthy  expects hostname "*"
```

Each one suppresses this warning. And because the same variable also gates the CORS allowlist (`api.ts:137`), and `isAllowedOrigin` has no `onrender.com` entry, the result isn't a write-only failure — it's a blank UI: no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on reads, 403 on writes, and *nothing* in the server log. The guard imports no logger, CORS denial is silent, and the one operator-facing signal has been switched off by the very misconfiguration that needed it.

A comma-separated value seems the most likely way in, since the sibling row one line below in the same README table documents "an Express-style list", and CORS allowlists are conventionally comma-separated — `GITNEXUS_MCP_ALLOWED_REPOS` (`README.md:518`) is documented as comma-separated and *fails startup* on bad entries. Worth matching that contract, or saying explicitly that only one origin is supported.

The hashed record carries `order | fromFile | targetRaw | result` — **not `files`**. A corpus edit that changes *which workspace* a case resolves against, while leaving the result string identical, is invisible to the gate.

Control: leaving the resolver **completely untouched** and editing only the corpus, two of the bench header's own documented load-bearing cases were gutted —

- `record(['deep/util/User.kt', 'util/User.kt'], 'util.User')` → `record(['util/User.kt'], 'util.User')`, so the "exact match anywhere beats a suffix match found earlier" case no longer tests the precedence rule at all (result string unchanged);
- `record(['data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt'], 'data.something')` → `record([], 'data.something')`, so the repeated-directory negative case loses its file entirely (still `NULL`).

Result: `cases 20074`, `non_null 11612`, fingerprint `5ad605c1…` — all byte-identical — and `[kotlin-import-target --check] PASS`. The advertised edge-case coverage can be deleted while CI stays green.

Fix is one line, then one deliberate re-baseline:
```js
lines.push(`${order}\t${list.join('|')}\t${fromFile}\t${targetRaw}\t${rendered}`);
```

**P1 — the corpus caps path depth at 8 components, and that is one of the three loops this PR added** `[reproduced]`

*A Claude adversarial lane + a coordinator control.*

This is one of the two deepest `DIRS` entries (`:202` is tied) — 7 directories + file. `buildCorpus` (`:248`) is pinned to the same shape, `lib<m>/src/main/kotlin/com/example/mod<m>/Class<i>.kt`. Real Android/Gradle source routinely runs 9–11 components.

Because of that, this mutation of `import-target.ts` passes `--check` with a **byte-identical** fingerprint, `cases`, *and* `non_null`:

```ts
const depthGuard = norm.split('/').length <= 8;
for (let i = 0; depthGuard && i < dir.length; i++) {   // skip deep paths
```

Measured against a standard Android/Gradle corpus (4 modules × 4 packages × 40 files, 9 components, 32 imports):

| | resolved to NULL | single-file | fan-outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| PR as written | 0 | 16 | 16 (avg 40 files) |
| with the mutation — **gate PASSES** | **16** | 16 | **0** |

Every package fan-out import resolves to `NULL` — the whole `#1759` multi-file tier dies — and CI is green. This is the same defect class #2794's C++ review found (its corpus drew every receiver from a declared namespace and was blind to the miss path) and fixed by widening the corpus.

Fix: add one `DIRS` entry at 10–12 components (e.g. `core/data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/core/data/repository`) plus a matching `record(...)` case resolved by suffix, and re-baseline once, deliberately.

**P1 — the corpus caps package size at 16 files, so a fan-out truncation is invisible** `[reproduced]`

*A Claude adversarial lane + a coordinator control.*

`3 + Math.floor(rnd() * 14)` tops out at 16, so no `dirChildren` bucket in the fuzz corpus ever exceeds 16 entries. A cap at 17 in the index build therefore changes nothing the gate can see:

```ts
else if (bucket.length < 17) bucket.push(raw);   // gate: cases 20074, non_null 11612, fingerprint 5ad605c1…, PASS
```

On the Android/Gradle corpus above, that silently truncates package fan-out from **40 candidate files to 17** — a 58% edge loss on every package import, with CI green.

This is not a hypothetical shape for this repo: a silent sibling cap is exactly what #2732 shipped on the JVM side.

Fix: raise `fileCount`, or add one explicit 40-file fan-out case above any plausible cap.

**P3 — the one place this PR is less documented than its own precedent** `[reproduced]`

*Claude: architecture, pattern-reuse, simplicity lanes. The Codex swarm leg reached the same conclusion independently.*

There is no note on why the shared `buildSuffixIndex` (`import-resolvers/utils.ts:90`, already used by C#, Ruby, Vue and TypeScript) isn't reused here. Python documents exactly this at `python/import-target.ts:214`.

The decision is **right** — run side by side, 4 of 5 probes diverge:

| probe | Kotlin | `buildSuffixIndex` |
|---|---|---|
| `['deep/util/User.kt','util/User.kt']` → `util.User` | `util/User.kt` | `deep/util/User.kt` — its single `exactMap` conflates exact and proper-suffix |
| `['deep/util/User.kt','util/User.kts']` → `util.User` | `util/User.kts` | `deep/util/User.kt` — keys carry the extension, so a `.kt` **suffix** beats a `.kts` **exact** |
| `['data/src/…/data/Repo.kt']` → `data.getRepo` | `null` | fan-out — `getFilesInDir` indexes *all* directory suffixes, with no first-occurrence rule |
| `['models/A.kts','models/B.kt']` → `models.getThing` | both, in set order | split into `:kt` and `:kts` buckets |

Three lines here stop the next person from "consolidating" it and silently moving edges — which matters because the PR body names Go, Dart and C#-no-csproj as next, and each will face the same question.
